page.text:
Exemplary mathematical writing rigorously maintains the transparency of
its logical dependencies. Before invoking a theorem, the author must
explicitly verify that all required hypotheses are satisfied in the
current context; before assigning a name to an object, its existence must
be confirmed; and before employing the definite article 'the', uniqueness
must be demonstrated.

These practices are not mere stylistic pedantry. They are the essential
safeguards that distinguish genuine deductive proof from persuasive yet
fallacious speculation, preserving the certainty that is the hallmark of
mathematical knowledge.
